Study and Improvement of Search Algorithms in Stochastic Perfect-Information Games

Quentin Cohen-Solal\corresponding    Tristan Cazenave
Abstract

In this article, we generalize Unbounded Minimax, the state-of-the-art search algorithm for deterministic zero-sum two-player games with perfect information to the framework of stochastic zero-sum two-player games with perfect information. We experimentally show that this generalized algorithm achieves better performance than the main stochastic search algorithms.

LAMSADE, Université@ Paris-Dauphine, PSL, CNRS, Paris, France

quentin.cohen-solal@dauphine.psl.eu

1 Introduction

Adversarial search in perfect-information games is a core domain of artificial intelligence, underpinning major theoretical and practical progress. In the case of two-player zero-sum games, algorithms such as Minimax and its many extensions provide a well-established framework for efficiently exploring large combinatorial state spaces. Among these approaches, Unbounded Minimax (Korf and Chickering 1996; Cohen-Solal 2026) has recently been identified as a state-of-the-art method (Cohen-Solal 2025).

Unlike traditional depth-limited minimax procedures, Unbounded Minimax conducts a best-first exploration of the most promising action sequences without imposing a predefined search horizon. Together with its safe decision variant (Cohen-Solal 2025), it constitutes the central search component of the Athénan architecture (Cohen-Solal 2026; Cohen-Solal 2020), a leading system in international game competitions. Over a six-year period, Athénan secured 57 gold medals at the Computer Olympiad (Cohen-Solal and Cazenave 2021; Cohen-Solal and Cazenave 2023a; Cohen-Solal and Cazenave 2025a), tripled the record for gold medals in a single year (Cohen-Solal and Cazenave 2023a), and held the title in 20 different games. Its primary competitor, AlphaZero (Silver et al. 2018), is based on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) (Coulom 2007). Experimental results indicate that, within comparable computational constraints, Athénan can outperform AlphaZero by up to a factor of 30 (Cohen-Solal and Cazenave 2023c).

Extending these successes to two-player stochastic games remains a significant challenge. Introducing stochasticity fundamentally alters the structure of the problem: the deterministic guarantees underlying classical adversarial search no longer hold, and the evaluation of positions must account for expected outcomes over chance events. As a result, several key properties of the deterministic setting are lost or weakened, including the straightforward propagation of exact minimax values.

These characteristics make direct extensions of algorithms designed for deterministic two-player zero-sum games insufficient. In particular, anticipating many turns ahead becomes considerably more difficult due to the exponential growth induced by chance nodes, often requiring approximations that can introduce substantial biases. Moreover, algorithms relying on precise value backpropagation must be adapted to handle expectations, which complicates both their theoretical analysis and practical behavior.

Furthermore, numerous algorithms have been proposed for stochastic two-player games, yet their relative performance remains poorly understood. It is still unclear whether a universally superior approach exists, even in terms of average performance, and under which conditions one method may outperform another.

In this paper, we introduce a novel search algorithm for stochastic two-player zero-sum games with perfect information, extending the Unbounded Minimax framework. The proposed method retains the core principles underlying the effectiveness of Unbounded Minimax—unbounded exploration, incremental resolution of states, and prioritization of the most critical action sequences—while explicitly incorporating stochastic transitions. This design helps control the combinatorial growth induced by chance nodes and supports deeper lookahead in such settings.

More precisely, our algorithmic contribution consists in transforming classical Expectiminimax, the standard search algorithm for stochastic games, into an anytime best-first search algorithm that generalizes Unbounded Minimax. Unlike classical Expectiminimax, which expands every chance outcome, Unbounded Expectiminimax expands only one sampled outcome per iteration, avoiding the exponential growth of the search tree due to chance and decision branching. At the same time, it preserves the exact expectiminimax backup operations rather than relying on Monte Carlo estimates as in MCTS.

We complement this contribution with an experimental evaluation on several benchmark stochastic games, showing that the proposed approach improves average performance compared to existing stochastic search methods and introduced variants.

Overall, these results contribute toward a unified perspective on adversarial search in two-player perfect-information games, encompassing both deterministic and stochastic settings while preserving strong empirical performance at scale.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    A generalization of Unbounded Minimax to stochastic games, resulting in the Unbounded Expectiminimax algorithm.

  • •

    An enhanced version of Unbounded Expectiminimax through the adaptation of two complementary techniques to stochastic games:

    • –

      the Safe Decision technique;

    • –

      the Completion technique.

  • •

    A large-scale empirical evaluation:

    • –

      across 8 stochastic games;

    • –

      using 30 independently trained evaluation functions per game, resulting in 30 × 30 network pairings for each domain;

    • –

      totaling 14,400 matches for each evaluated algorithm.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review related work, covering Unbounded Minimax and classical stochastic game algorithms. Section 3.1 formalizes our new generalized search algorithms: Unbounded Expectiminimax and Unbounded Expectiminimax with safe decision. In Section 3.2, we describe our experimental protocol, including the evaluation setup, technical details, and the set of games considered. We then present its results in Section 3.3. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future work.

2 Related Work

2.1 Best Action Searching in Game Trees

The vast majority of game-search algorithms rely on representing a game as a tree, where nodes correspond to game states and edges correspond to actions that allow transitions from one state to another. The terminal nodes represent end-game states and are assigned a value according to the final game outcome. Typically v∈{−1,0,1}v\in\left\{-1,0,1\right\} where v=1v=1 means the first player wins, v=0v=0 means draw, and v=−1v=-1 means the first player loses (and thus the second player wins). More generally, v∈ℝv\in\mathbb{R} and vv is the score of the first player. This valuation can be propagated to the other nodes under the assumption that both players play optimally. However, this theoretical valuation is generally intractable in practice, as game trees represent enormous state spaces. Consequently, algorithms must estimate these values or the corresponding strategies to make practical game-playing decisions.

2.2 Base Stochastic Search: Expectiminimax

The Expectiminimax algorithm (Michie 1966) is the canonical approach for stochastic zero-sum two-player games: it constructs a game tree to a fixed depth, evaluates the leaf nodes with a heuristic evaluation function, and propagates these values back up the tree under the assumption that the first player maximizes its payoff, that the second player minimizes the first player payoff, and that stochastic events follow the probabilities defined by the game. Expectiminimax remains the simplest and most fundamental framework for reasoning about stochastic two-player adversarial behavior.

When upper and lower bounds on the values of horizon states are known, a pruning generalizing the alpha-beta technique can be used; this technique is called *-minimax (Ballard 1983). Our study is not situated within this specific setting.

2.3 Monte-Carlo Tree Search

Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) (Browne et al. 2012; Coulom 2007) reframed game search for domains where hand-crafted evaluation functions are inadequate. Instead of evaluating every leaf node with a heuristic, MCTS performs randomized simulations (playouts) and uses their outcomes to guide a best-first expansion of the search tree through four iterative steps: selection, expansion, simulation, and backpropagation. MCTS has achieved remarkable success across a wide range of board and real-time games. MCTS\mathrm{MCTS} is parameterized by a constant CC which needs to be tuned (theoretical value 2\sqrt{2}).

It has also been modified in various ways to incorporate knowledge to improve its performance by biasing its selections and/or simulations (Browne et al. 2012). The simplest method is to replace state evaluation by playouts with heuristic evaluation (Ramanujan and Selman 2011). We denote this variant by MCTSh\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}.

Using MCTS in stochastic games introduces chance nodes. Two generalisations are commonly considered. The first proceeds with selection until a state is reached that is not present in the tree, regardless of whether it is a chance or a decision node. The second continues exploration until a previously unseen decision node is encountered (OpenSpiel contributors 2025). In this variant, chance nodes are always fully expanded according to the game’s probability distribution and are not evaluated by the evaluation function (when such a function is used). We denote this variant as MCTSh′\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}{}^{\prime}.

Open-loop MCTS (Perez Liebana et al. 2015) is a variant of Monte Carlo Tree Search that evaluates action sequences rather than state-action pairs, thereby avoiding explicit dependence on exact state identities. It is particularly suited to stochastic or partially observable environments, where different states can lead to similar action distributions, and it improves scalability by aggregating statistics over action histories instead of full state representations. We denote this variant using heuristic evaluation by MCTShopen\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}^{\text{open}}.

2.4 Unbounded Minimax and Safe Decision

Unbounded Minimax

Unbounded (Best-First) Minimax (Cohen-Solal 2025; Korf and Chickering 1996; Cohen-Solal and Cazenave 2025b; Cohen-Solal 2026; Cohen-Solal 2021) is an extension of the classical Minimax, the base algorithm for two-player zero-sum games with perfect information. In its standard form, Minimax explores the game tree uniformly up to a fixed depth dd, assuming both players act optimally within this search horizon, one maximizing the payoff and the other minimizing it. This approach, however, quickly becomes intractable as dd increases, due to the exponential growth of the search space.

To overcome this limitation, Unbounded Minimax replaces depth-limited exploration with a best-first, non-uniform search strategy. Instead of expanding the entire frontier, it focuses selectively on the most promising parts of the search space, enabling significantly deeper local exploration. Concretely, the algorithm identifies the currently best sequence of actions, extends it by one step, and iteratively repeats this process. Unlike standard Minimax, it does not rely on a predefined depth parameter: the search progresses incrementally and can be stopped at any time while still providing a valid solution.

Safe Unbounded Minimax

Unbounded Minimax was later extended with the safe decision technique (Cohen-Solal 2025; Cohen-Solal 2026), which modifies the final action-selection rule while leaving the underlying search procedure unchanged. In the standard version, the selected action is the one leading to the child state with the highest evaluated value. In contrast, the safe decision strategy selects the action deemed the safest, defined as the one most frequently chosen during the search.

More precisely, the selected action maximizes the number of times that action has been preferred at the root throughout the search process. Given that the exploration follows a best-first strategy, this action corresponds to the one most often identified as optimal during successive iterations. This mechanism improves robustness to evaluation inaccuracies. Additionally, it favors the action for which the algorithm has explored the deepest and most extensively developed subtree, thereby providing greater insight into its potential future outcomes.

Unbounded Minimax with Completion

Unbounded Minimax has also been enhanced through the completion technique (Cohen-Solal 2021; Cohen-Solal 2026). This extension introduces two key improvements. First, it prunes actions leading to solved states, i.e., states whose exact value is known and cannot be altered by further exploration, thereby preventing the search from being trapped in suboptimal fixed points. Second, it refines the final decision rule by systematically prioritizing actions that lead to solved winning states and, whenever possible, avoiding those that lead to solved losing states.

3 Contributions

3.1 A New Search Algorithm for Stochastic Games

In this section, we introduce our generalization of Unbounded Minimax to the stochastic setting. We call this algorithm Unbounded Expectiminimax. Like Unbounded Minimax for deterministic games, this algorithm iteratively extends the a priori best action sequence as long as search time remains, except that in added chance states, the next state is chosen at random and that the values of states are no longer the minimax value but the expectiminimax value (of the partial game tree).

In contrast to classic Expectiminimax, our algorithm mitigates the combinatorial explosion induced by chance nodes. It expands only a single sampled successor at each chance node per iteration, progressively refining value estimates through repeated sampling. This approach combines the scalability of sampling-based methods, which avoid exhaustive expansion, with the principled backup mechanism of Expectiminimax, which preserves correctness when exact evaluations are available.

At each iteration, the algorithm performs a recursive selection from the root (the current game state), descending the tree according to the following decision rules: in max nodes (first-player states), it selects the child with maximal value; in min nodes (second-player states), the child with minimal value; and in chance nodes, a successor is sampled according to the probability distribution defined by the game. This process continues until a leaf of the current partial tree is reached, at which point expansion occurs: the newly encountered state is added to the search tree. Then, value updates are propagated backward.

During backpropagation, node values are updated according to their type: max nodes take the maximum over their children, min nodes the minimum, and chance nodes the expectation over their children weighted by their transition probabilities. This procedure is repeated from the root for the available search budget, yielding an anytime algorithm that progressively improves its decision quality over time.

The completion technique is generalized as follows: at the end of the search, always play an action that is resolved as winning with probability 11, and, if possible, never play an action that is resolved as losing with probability 11. Thus, an action resolved as winning with probability p<1p<1 is not necessarily played. A state is considered resolved if all its children are resolved, or if it has a winning action for the current player with probability 11. Finally, during the search, a resolved action is never explored. An action aa in a state ss is marked as resolved when rs,a=1r_{s,a}=1 (otherwise rs,a=0r_{s,a}=0). An action aa in a state ss is marked as resolved winning with probability 11 when cs,a=1c_{s,a}=1. An action aa in a state ss is marked as resolved losing with probability 11 when cs,a=−1c_{s,a}=-1.

The Unbounded Expectiminimax algorithm for stochastic games (with completion and optionally with safe decision) is described in Algorithm 1.

3.2 Experimental Study of Stochastic Searches

We now present the experiments conducted to evaluate the contributions of this paper. We will present its results in the following section (Section 3.3).

We begin by presenting the experimental protocol (Section 3.2). Then we explain how the evaluation functions used by the search algorithms were generated (Section 3.2). Next, we describe the computer used (Section 3.2), and finally present the other details of the experiment (Section 3.2).

Evaluation Protocol

We experimentally compare the following algorithms: (classic) Expectiminimax, MCTS\mathrm{MCTS}, MCTSh\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}, MCTShopen\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}^{\text{open}}, MCTSh′\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}{}^{\prime}, Unbounded Expectiminimax with classic decision and with safe decision.

We use standard Expectiminimax as benchmark adversary using a lossless parallelization procedure, called Child Batching (Cohen-Solal 2025; Cohen-Solal 2026) (child Batching consists in evaluating the children states of states in parallel by the neural network). We evaluate each algorithm on the following 8 games: Azul, Kingdomino, Mighty Duel Kingdomino, Can’t Stop, Backgammon, EinStein würfelt nicht!, Shogun, and Martian Dice. Corresponding descriptions are in Appendix.

Each algorithm faces the benchmark adversary 22 times: once in first player and once in second player. These matches are repeated 30×3030\times 30 times: we use a set of 30 evaluation functions per game in order to assess the algorithms statistically. More precisely, each algorithm is evaluated for each evaluation function fif_{i} (i∈{0,…,29}i\in\left\{0,\ldots,29\right\}) that it uses and for each opponent evaluation function fjf_{j} (j∈{0,…,29}j\in\left\{0,\ldots,29\right\}). In other words, for all i,j∈{0,…,,29}i,j\in\left\{0,\ldots,,29\right\}, the evaluated algorithm using fif_{i} confronts in a same match the following opponent: the benchmark adversary with the evaluation fjf_{j}. This corresponds to 1800 matches per game for each evaluated algorithm. The performance evaluation of an algorithm for a specific game is therefore based on this number of matches. The performance of a search algorithm is the average of the binary scores obtained at the end of its matches (1 for a victory, 0 for a draw and -1 for a defeat).

Each search algorithm uses the same search time: 10 seconds per action (order of magnitude of search time in competition).

Each algorithm is evaluated with and without Completion. For MCTS and classic Expectiminimax, this means always playing a solved action with a 100% winning probability and never a solved action with a 100% losing probability after the search. Unbounded Expectiminimax, in addition, never selects a solved action during the search. This sub-technique is irrelevant for classic Expectiminimax and significantly reduces performance for Monte Carlo Tree Search (Winands et al. 2008) (we have also verified this in the context of this experiment : it decreases by 25%25\% the performance).

The evaluated algorithms do not use Child Batching, unlike their opponent. We do not use it because Child Batching cannot be applied to MCTS algorithms, as they do not evaluate all children of a state sequentially. Although some form of parallelization is possible, it comes at the cost of performance, and parallelization is not the focus of this paper. To ensure a fair comparison, we therefore disable Child Batching for all evaluated algorithms.

Note, however, that Expectiminimax-based algorithms, including both the classical algorithm and our unbounded variants, can make use of Child Batching. This improves their absolute performance, but does not alter their relative performance. Child Batching increases the performance of Expectiminimax algorithms by around 6%6\%.

Evaluation Functions Training

We now present how the evaluation functions used in the experiments of this paper were learned.

The evaluation functions were generated using Athénan (Cohen-Solal 2026) ; the reinforcement learning algorithm, by replacing its core component Descent Minimax, with its generalization for stochastic games: Descent Expectiminimax (Cohen-Solal and Cazenave 2023b).

Athénan involves sequentially performing self-play matches using the learned evaluation function to guide the search process, deciding which actions to take during the matches and how to explore the search tree. The data encountered (the associations states-values) is then learned at the end of each match to update the evaluation function. This thus forms a self-improving loop.

The Athénan hyperparameters used to generate each evaluation function are the following: search time per action t=2​st=2s, batch size B=3000B=3000, duplication factor δ=3\delta=3, memory size M=50M=50, the selection action method is still the ordinal law but its parameter is X\sqrt{X} with XX a uniform random variable in [0,1], neural network optimizer: Adam (Kingma and Ba 2014) with λ=0.0001\lambda=0.0001 as learning rate. The neural network architecture used is as follow: a convolutional layer, 88 residual blocks (He et al. 2016) (containing 2 convolutional layers), a flatten layer, two dense layers with NN neurons (see Table 2) , and a final dense layer with 11 neuron (the output). Each convolutional layer has CC channels (see Table 2) The activation function is the ReLU.

Each of the evaluation functions is the result of 10 days of training.

Computer Used

We provide details of the machines used in the experiments described in this article.

We used the LUMI-G partition of the LUMI Supercomputer. A process uses 7 AMD Trento CPU with 64 GB of RAM and 1 AMD MI250 GPU with 64 GB of RAM.

Other Details of the Experiment

We give for each algorithm: the average performance over all games, the associated 95% stratified bootstrapping confidence interval (lower and upper bound) and the performance for each game with its 95% confidence radius. The percentages detailing performance for each game have been rounded to the nearest percent to reduce size and improve readability of data tables.

Algorithms based on a fixed search depth (classic Expectiminimax) use iterative deepening (Korf 1985) to be parameterized by a search time.

All algorithms use transposition tables (Greenblatt et al. 1988). This allows the game tree to be transformed into a directed acyclic graph, which therefore simplifies the state space.

The evaluation functions for MCTSh\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}} need to take values in [0,1][0,1]. We use the following normalization to obtain such evaluation functions, transforming an evaluation function ff with values in ℝ\mathbb{R} into an evaluation function fnf_{\mathrm{n}} with values in [0,1][0,1]:

fn​(s)=max⁡(min⁡(f⁡(s),M),m)−mM−mf_{\mathrm{n}}(s)=\frac{\max\left(\min\left(f\left(s\right),M\right),m\right)-m}{M-m}

with ss a game state, ff the state evaluation function, MM the maximum practical value for ff, mm the minimum practical value of ff. More formally, M=max⁡VM=\max V and m=min⁡Vm=\min V with V={f⁡(s′)|s′∈S}V=\left\{f\left(s^{\prime}\right)\,|\,s^{\prime}\in S\right\} where SS is a set of states from matches played using ff generated during 24 hours.

3.3 Results of the Experimental Study

We now present the results of the experiment. In Section 3.3, we present the performance of algorithms with a medium search time per action. In Section 3.3, we present the performance of algorithms with a short search time per action.

Comparison with a Medium Search Time

We thus evaluate the following algorithms: MCTS\mathrm{MCTS}, MCTSh\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}, MCTShopen\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}^{\text{open}}, MCTSh′\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}{}^{\prime} and Unbounded Expectiminimax with and without Safe Decision, and classic Expectiminimax. The algorithms performances are described in Table 4 (mean over the games) and Table 3 (details).

Overall, Unbounded Expectiminimax with and without safe decision achieves similar results, indistinguishable within the confidence interval (both with and without completion). This contrasts with the deterministic case, where safe decision substantially improves performance. In contrast, as in the deterministic setting, Completion significantly improves performance, by approximately 8%8\%. The Unbounded Expectiminimax algorithms generally outperform all other algorithms. Classic Expectiminimax achieves results comparable to MCTSh\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}} and MCTSh′\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}^{{}^{\prime}} without Completion but it is stronger with completion. Evaluating chance nodes with MCTSh\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}} has only a very limited impact on performance. On the other hand, the open-loop variant performs significantly worse. The worst-performing algorithm overall is MCTS\mathrm{MCTS}, i.e. without the use of learned knowledge (showing that learning is indeed beneficial and has a strong impact on performance).

We now examine the results in greater detail on a game-by-game basis, highlighting the points where the observed behavior diverges from the overall trend.

In Azul without using Completion, Monte Carlo approaches using learned knowledge perform best. In particular, MCTSh\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}} achieves the best results. However, adding Completion greatly improves Unbounded Expectiminimax, which is not the case with MCTS, and Unbounded Expectiminimax with Completion achieves the performance of MCTSh\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}.

In Backgammon, Martian Dice, and Einstein würfelt nicht!, completion has no measurable impact.

In Azul, safe decision significantly improves performance in this setting, whereas it significantly decreases performance in Einstein würfelt nicht!.

Comparison with a Short Search

In this section, we repeat the main experiment of the paper using a short search time (1 second).

We thus evaluate the following algorithms in this modified context: MCTS\mathrm{MCTS}, MCTSh\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}, MCTShopen\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}^{\text{open}}, MCTSh′\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}{}^{\prime} and Unbounded Expectiminimax with and without Safe Decision, and classic Expectiminimax. The algorithms’ performances are summarized in Table 5, which reports the average performance across games. Detailed results for each individual game are provided in Appendix Table 6.

We recover the main conclusions observed in the 10-second setting (Safe Unbounded Expectiminimax without Completion is more efficient than classic Expectiminimax, MCTSh\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}} and MCTSh′\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}^{{}^{\prime}} which are more efficient than MCTShopen\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}^{\text{open}}, itself more efficient than MCTS\mathrm{MCTS}; Completion improves performance).

There are, however, two notable global differences:

  • •

    Safe decision improves performance, as in the deterministic case (although the effect is less pronounced).

  • •

    MCTSh\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}} outperforms MCTSh′\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}}^{{}^{\prime}}: evaluating chance states therefore improves performance.

Regarding game-specific observations that diverge from the overall behavior, we observe several results that are consistent with those reported previously in the 10-second setting:

  • •

    In Azul, safe decision significantly improves performance, whereas it significantly decreases performance in Einstein würfelt nicht!.

  • •

    In Backgammon, Martian Dice, and Einstein würfelt nicht!, completion still has no measurable impact.

There are, however, some game-specific differences:

  • •

    In Can’t Stop, without Completion, MCTSh\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}} is the best-performing algorithm.

  • •

    In the 10-second setting for Azul, without Completion, MCTSh\mathrm{MCTS}_{\mathrm{h}} was the best-performing algorithm. This is no longer the case here, as Unbounded Expectiminimax with safe decision achieves the best results.

  • •

    In Kingdomino, Mighty Duel Kingdomino, and Shogun, safe decision significantly improves performance.

4 Discussion

Beyond the empirical results, the design of Unbounded Expectiminimax highlights several key differences with both classical Expectiminimax and Monte-Carlo Tree Search. These differences provide insights into the conditions under which Unbounded Expectiminimax may be particularly effective and suggest possible explanations for its observed performance.

Rather than approximating expectiminimax values through stochastic rollouts, Unbounded Expectiminimax preserves the exact expectiminimax backup operation. As a result, the quality of the search depends primarily on the accuracy of the evaluation function rather than on Monte-Carlo estimation variance. In the ideal case of a perfect evaluation function, the optimal action can be identified after a single iteration, whereas MCTS must still reduce rollout variance through repeated simulations.

Another important consequence is that Unbounded Expectiminimax naturally inherits the best-first search behavior of Unbounded Minimax. Instead of distributing the search effort uniformly across the game tree, it concentrates computation on the most promising branches. This selective expansion enables the algorithm to reach strategically deeper positions under a fixed computational budget, provided that the evaluation function is sufficiently informative.

The proposed tree construction strategy also changes the computational characteristics of expectiminimax search. Classical Expectiminimax expands all successors of every chance node, leading to exponential growth of the search tree and requiring iterative deepening to provide intermediate decisions. In contrast, Unbounded Expectiminimax expands only one sampled outcome at each iteration, making the number of newly expanded nodes per iteration independent of the branching factors of decision and chance nodes, while remaining an anytime algorithm without additional computation.

Finally, unlike MCTS, Unbounded Expectiminimax does not rely on an explicit exploration–exploitation trade-off or on Monte-Carlo value estimation. The search is entirely driven by backed-up expectiminimax values, eliminating the need for exploration constants or other search hyperparameters. This makes the search procedure parameter-free and simplifies its practical application across different stochastic games without domain-specific tuning.

Overall, these properties suggest that Unbounded Expectiminimax is particularly well suited to stochastic games where reasonably accurate evaluation functions are available. In such settings, replacing exhaustive chance-node expansion with repeated sampling preserves the strengths of Expectiminimax while substantially improving its scalability and anytime behavior.

Our experimental results are consistent with this analysis and show that evaluation functions sufficiently informative to make Unbounded Expectiminimax the best-performing algorithm can be obtained with only a few days of computation on a GPU.

5 Conclusion

In this paper, we investigated search algorithms for stochastic perfect-information games. We generalized Unbounded Minimax with Safe Decision and Completion, a state-of-the-art approach for deterministic two-player zero-sum perfect-information games, to the stochastic setting, resulting in Unbounded Expectiminimax and its variants.

We evaluated these algorithms through a large-scale empirical study against the main stochastic search algorithms from the literature. Our results show that our generalizations achieve the best average performance for medium search times. Unlike in deterministic settings, however, Safe Decision does not consistently provide a significant improvement over the classical decision rule. Their performances are generally close, and in one game the classical decision rule performs substantially better. Completion, in contrast, consistently improves performance.

We also evaluated the algorithms under a shorter search budget (1 second). The results are consistent with those obtained for medium search times (10 seconds), with the difference that Safe Decision provides additional improvements in this setting.

Across both search budgets, Unbounded Expectiminimax achieves the best average performance among all evaluated stochastic search algorithms. This work extends the unbounded best-first search paradigm from deterministic to stochastic perfect-information games, providing a unified framework covering both settings.

Overall, our results suggest that Unbounded Expectiminimax with Safe Decision is a strong default choice for stochastic perfect-information games when an accurate evaluation function is available or can be learned, for example through several days of GPU-based training. In some specific cases, such as particular games or search budgets, the classical decision rule can still provide competitive or superior performance.

Future work will investigate the extension of this framework to multiplayer and imperfect-information games.

5.2 Games

We present in this section the games on which we conduct our comparison experiments for search algorithms, namely EinStein würfelt nicht!, Backgammon, Azul, Kingdomino, Mighty Duel Kingdomino, Martian Dice, Shogun, and Can’t Stop. A comparison of the different characteristics of these games, namely state space estimation, proportion of chance estimation, and BoardGameGeek game rating, is provided in Table 15.

EinStein Würfelt Nicht!

We start by presenting the game EinStein würfelt nicht!.

This game is played on a 5×55\times 5 square board. The objective is to reach with one of his pieces his arrival position which is the square of the corner of the board located in the opponent’s starting area. The two starting areas are described in Figure 1. The game has an initialization phase where the players will place their 6 pieces on the board. Each player’s pieces are numbered from 1 to 6. During the initialization phase, the pieces are arranged randomly but symmetrically with respect to the games (central symmetry). Then a race phase starts. As soon as a player reaches his arrival square with one of his pieces, the game is over. At the start of each turn, during the race phase, a 6-sided die is rolled. It indicates the current player’s piece that he can move (the one with the same number as the result of the die). If there is no piece on the board corresponding to the number on the die, the piece to be moved is the one whose number is closest to the result of the die. If there are two possibilities, the player chooses. A piece’s possible move is one of three moves to an adjacent square that bring the piece closer to that player’s arrival square (horizontal move, vertical move, or diagonal move). If the piece ends its movement on another piece (no matter which player it belongs to), the other piece is removed from the board.

We use these rules in this paper (they are the Computer Olympiad rules). However, variants do exist, with respect to the initialization phase, where for example the first player places his pieces in his starting area and then the second player places his pieces in his starting area symmetrically (Polygames rules (Cazenave et al. 2020)). In the Ludii (Piette et al. 2020) implementation, during the initialization phase, in turn, each player places one of his pieces in his starting area.

Despite its great simplicity and the element of luck, it is a game that has tactics and strategies.

The more recent programs at EinStein würfelt nicht! are based on MCTS (Chen et al. 2023; Chu et al. 2017; Lu et al. 2015; Lorentz 2011). There are also works on endgame tablebase (Turner 2012) and on solving EinStein würfelt nicht! (Bonnet and Viennot 2017).

According to the BoardGameGeek community, EinStein würfelt nicht! ranks as the 600th-best abstract game and 14,827th overall.

Backgammon

Backgammon is one of the oldest known board games, with origins estimated to date back to around 3000 BCE. Backgammon provides a long-standing benchmark for evaluating decision-making under uncertainty in stochastic perfect-information games (Tesauro 2002; Van Lishout et al. 2007; Pollack et al. 1997).

Backgammon is played on a board of 24 triangular points. Each player starts with 15 checkers. The objective is to be the first player to bear off all of one’s checkers from the board. On each turn, a player rolls two dice and must move checkers according to the dice values. A checker may move to an open point (unoccupied or occupied by the player’s own checkers) or to a point occupied by exactly one opponent checker, in which case the opponent checker is hit and placed on the bar. Checkers on the bar must re-enter the board before any other move can be played. Once all of a player’s checkers are in their home board (the last six points), they may begin bearing off checkers according to the dice rolls. Complete rules of Backgammon are available at boardgamegeek.com (BoardGameGeek contributors 2021).

Historically, Backgammon played a central role in demonstrating the effectiveness of temporal-difference learning with neural networks, most notably through Tesauro’s TD-Gammon (Tesauro 1995; Tesauro 2002), which reached strong human-expert level using self-play and function approximation. AlphaZero also reaches this success recently (Antonoglou et al. 2021). Deciding whether a player can win at Backgammon is EXPTIME-Hard (Witter 2021).

According to the BoardGameGeek community, Backgammon ranks as the 141st-best abstract game and 1,641st overall.

Azul

Azul is a game featuring chaining, grid coverage, open drafting, pattern building, and set collection mechanics. The core mechanics of Azul consist of drafting 5 groups of 4 randomly drawn colored tiles and placing them on a personal board to maximize points under geometric placement constraints, while managing penalties and strategic risk arising from indirect opponent interaction and chance. Rules of Azul are available at boardgamegeek.com (Plan B Games Inc. 2018).

According to the BoardGameGeek community, Azul has a complexity comparable to Backgammon, ranks as the second-best abstract game and 97th overall. It has sold over two million copies worldwide, and won both the Spiel des Jahres and the As d’Or (game of the year) in 2018, two of the most prestigious awards in the board game industry.

The mechanics of Azul have been analyzed, showing that they promote indirect and continuous sabotage through resource denial while maintaining a balance between individual optimization and competitive player interaction (Acatrinei and Brinza 2024).

Kingdomino

Kingdomino is a game featuring enclosure, open drafting, and domino placement mechanics for two, three, and four players.

The core gameplay consists of sequentially drafting four randomly drawn domino-like tiles and placing them within a growing 5×55\times 5 grid, subject to adjacency constraints. A distinctive feature of Kingdomino is its coupled action mechanism: each player selects one domino, which directly determines that player’s position in the next turn order. The more valuable a tile a player chooses, the worse their ranking will be in the next round, and the fewer choices they will have at that point. This introduces a trade-off between immediate reward (high-value tiles) and strategic positioning (earlier versus later turn order), creating a delayed and interdependent decision process. In addition, scoring is non-linear, depending on the formation of connected domino regions of the same landscape weighted by “crown” multipliers, found on certain tiles. Rules of Kingdomino are available at boardgamegeek.com (BoardGameGeek contributors 2016).

One variant, called Mighty Duel, allows one to play on a 7×77\times 7 board. Both 5×55\times 5 and 7×77\times 7 variants are used as benchmarks in the experiments presented in this paper.

In addition, the two variants studied use the following advanced rules: “Middle Kingdom” and “Harmony”, which add additional end-game scoring objectives related to tile placement.

It is NP-complete to decide whether a given score is achievable at Kingdomino (Nguyen et al. 2020). An experimental study on multiplayer search algorithms was conducted on Kingdomino (with four players) (Gedda et al. 2018).

Kingdomino notably won the Spiel des Jahres in 2017. According to the BoardGameGeek community, Kingdomino ranks as the 80th-best family game and 329th overall.

Martian Dice

Martian Dice offers a lightweight yet informative benchmark for evaluating reinforcement learning and planning algorithms in stochastic games. Although simpler than classical board games, it isolates core challenges of decision-making under uncertainty: notably risk management and more precisely the Push your luck dilemma. Each turn consists of repeated roll-and-choose decisions, where an agent must determine whether to stop and secure its current score or continue rolling to pursue higher payoff at the risk of losing his recent gains.

In Martian Dice, players take on the role of Martians trying to abduct humans, cows, and chickens from Earth. Each turn, a player rolls 13 custom dice showing different symbols: humans, cows, chickens, Earth’s tanks, and death rays. After each roll, all tanks must be set aside. The player then chooses one additional type to keep (one kind of Earthling to abduct or death rays to defend against tanks), and rerolls the remaining dice. This continues until all dice are set aside or decide to stop. At the end of the turn, if the player has at least as many death rays as tanks, the abductions are successful and the kept Earthlings are scored. A bonus is awarded if the player manages to abduct at least one human, one cow, and one chicken in the same turn. Complete rules are available at boardgamegeek.com (BoardGameGeek contributors 2011).

The game is characterized by very limited player choices contrasted with highly diverse random events, making it a particular case interesting as benchmark for approximate decision-making methods.

According to the BoardGameGeek community, Martian Dice ranks as the 1,353rd-best game.

Can’t Stop

Can’t Stop is a game featuring push your luck, race, roll and move, track movement mechanics.

In Can’t Stop, players roll four dice each turn and combine them into pairs to advance markers up columns corresponding to dice sums. There are 12 columns, each with a different difficulty. Players may iteratively continue rolling to progress further or stop to secure their gains, but risk losing all progress from the turn if no valid move is possible. The goal is to be the first to complete three columns. Complete rules are available at boardgamegeek.com (BoardGameGeek contributors 2003).

According to the BoardGameGeek community, Can’t Stop ranks as the 217th-best family game and 765th overall.

Shogun

Shogun (1976) is played on an 8×88\times 8 board with pawns and a king, aiming to capture the opponent’s pieces by moving onto their squares. Each piece displays a number indicating how far it can move, and this value changes randomly after each movement. Its complete rules are available on Ludii (Piette et al. 2020).

According to the BoardGameGeek community, Shogun has a complexity comparable to Backgammon and ranks as the 1,074th-best family game and 13,466th overall.
